lesson_title: The Graph That Lies: Reading Data Displays
hook_text: "Winter electricity use TRIPLES." It went up 10 percent. Here's exactly how the picture lied.
clip_script: A family buys prepaid electricity. May: 410 units. June: 450 units. Now a newspaper draws those two as bars — but starts the bottom of the axis at 390 instead of zero. Watch what happens. May has 20 units sticking up above the line. June has 60. Three times as tall. Headline: electricity use triples. It did not. It went up 40 units on 410 — that's about 10 out of every 100, roughly 10 percent. The numbers never lied. The picture did, by chopping the bottom off the axis. And once you know the trick you'll spot it everywhere. A pie chart tilted in three dimensions makes the front slice look fatter than an equal slice at the back. A little picture drawn twice as tall AND twice as wide looks four times as big — but only stands for double. So before you believe any graph: where does the scale start, are the gaps even, is every axis labelled, and is the total actually given? Make your eyes wait for the numbers.
visual_style: Two bars on a clean axis; the axis baseline slides up from 0 to 390 and the bars stretch grotesquely, then snap back as the true 10 percent gap appears; quick beats of a tilted pie and a doubling pictogram.
mood: Sharp, slightly conspiratorial — the pleasure of catching someone out.
pacing: Slow reveal on the sliding axis, rapid-fire on the other tricks, firm four-question close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never be fooled by a picture of numbers again.
